B.10 WOODY BIOMASS | GASIFICATION | DME DME is conventionally produced via methanol dehydration (Zhu et al., 2009). In this process, the semi-purified methanol (about 98%) produced from biomass gasification is used as the feed of the DME synthesis reactor. In the reactor, methanol is dehydrated over 𝛾-Al O catalyst. The reactor 2 3 outlet contains DME, water, and unreacted methanol, which are separated via distillation. The unreacted methanol is recycled back to the reactor. B.11 CORN STARCH | FERMENTATION | ETHANOL Corn to ethanol is a well-established process and majority of ethanol in United States is produced from corn via fermentation. Ground corn is added along with recycle water, alpha-amylase, ammonia, and caustic/lime. The stream is further cooled to 60°C before saccharification where glucoamylase is added with sulfuric acid for pH control. The effluent from saccharification is cooled before feeding to four continuous cascade fermenters where yeast is fed. Exhaust gas from the fermenters is vented to the vent scrubber. At the end of the fermentation train, the fermented beer and scrubber bottoms are collected. The effective ethanol concentration in the fermentation train is 10–13 vol %. Distillation and molecular sieve adsorption are used to recover and concentrate ethanol from the raw fermentation beer and produce 99.5% ethanol. The heated beer is then fed to the beer column, which removes residual carbon dioxide and as little ethanol as possible overhead. Ethanol is removed as a vapor side draw from the beer column and fed directly to the rectification column. Overhead from the rectification column is fed to the molecular sieve unit. Adsorption removes 95% of the water and a small portion of ethanol. The 99.5% pure ethanol vapor is cooled by heat exchange against regenerated condensate and finally condensed and pumped to offsite storage. B-3 The beer column bottoms stream, which contains all the unfermented, nonvolatile components, is known as whole stillage. After heat interchange, the whole stillage is sent to distillers’ dried grains recovery as a coproduct. B.12 CORN STOVER | FERMENTATION | ETHANOL Corn stover is lignocellulosic agricultural waste that is available in large quantities in the United States. The process adopted in this work is based on the National Renewable Energy Laboratory’s lignocellulose feedstock to ethanol technology (Humbird et al., 2011), using co-current dilute acid pre-hydrolysis of the lignocellulosic biomass with simultaneous enzymatic saccharification of the remaining cellulose and co-fermentation of the resulting glucose and xylose to ethanol. Specifically, the stover is first pretreated to hydrolyze hemicellulose to soluble sugars with the help of dilute sulfuric at 190°C. About 90% of the hemicellulose is converted to xylose. Then simultaneous saccharification and co-fermentation of the hydrolysate slurry is carried out in a series of continuous anaerobic fermentation trains where enzymes and other nutrients are added.
